utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. Apologise for the good weather outside and we having to work in here. Without any delay, could we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the OTP, the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we continue immediately with the examination-in-chief, hopefully to be concluded today. Is there a realistic chance?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It depends on Your Honours rulings over documents, basically speaking. But Your Honour I want to come back to the document yesterday that Your Honour raised some questions about. We obtained from the evidence vault the original. The document has the 65 ter number 239.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it be presented to the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps I may explain and then hand it over. Your Honour queried what these documents were. In fact, they are two copies, if that's the right word, of the same telex it would appear. The first one that appears in the bundle with the number 00478710 was, in fact, recovered from Sanski Most. It was attached to this exhibit because it was the same. But the one that was recovered from the Prijedor Police Station, Your Honour, is the second document in the bundle which, in fact, is one long telex. It's one document that has been put on to two pages. So Your Honour, I'll hand that out for the Defence and Your Honours to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that in the future, it would really facilitate the proceedings if we have this most original document before us, and it facilitates the understanding. But I think it's necessary because the translation never can serve as a document admitted into evidence. It's only the document, and then the copies for the purpose of our case only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it was my error on not checking. I'm afraid I tend to look at the English translation only, and I hadn't checked the B/C/S version of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that we don't lose time, I think it's necessary to give provisional numbers. I state that yesterday we came to 149, so this would be, then, provisionally 150B, 150B, the long exhibit with the number 00633169.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't ask for the other document to be exhibited because the only relevance is that the first one was found in the Prijedor Police Station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. And once again, this would facilitate our work because of this long document, even if to a certain extent confusing, we have the translation into English before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Similarly to those that we raised previously, this concerns a Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, not the purported Crisis Staff in Prijedor. This is a facsimile which doesn't indicate that it received or sent to anyone in the Prijedor area, specifically the accused here, Dr. Stakic. And we'll also incorporate our prior objections as to relevancy, Your Honour, and foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to, in fact, go back, ask the witness to look at it because I want to ask him a question as to what's stated there. And as to it being shown that there's any connection with the accused or where it comes from, if it is found at the Prijedor Police Station, Your Honour, we would suggest that that is sufficient foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I apologise. And that's our specific point. Your Honour, they had a gentleman by the name of Mr. Inayat here, who testified only in part. If counsel's going to give testimony, we would also like to be given the opportunity to testify. We're not attacking the veracity of what counsel says, but the foundation has to be laid properly, legally, and formally, not merely by lawyers suggesting that it was found in Prijedor because there is a specific stamp or a specific what we call the little mini yellow sheet placed on the document identifying it as being the document found in Prijedor Police Station by one of the OTP prosecutors himself, Michael Keegan. That was an issue raised in some of the questions but not completed, because the testimony by Mr. Inayat was not complete. By virtue of the comments made now by the OTP, it is quite clear that the foundation has not been properly laid for this as well as other documents. We can accept it provisionally, but I certainly would want an indication from the Court if we can resist or have both parties resist from giving factual or legal conclusions on documents that are required by law for them to prove through witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think here we have to come down to earth. I can't see the big problem in this question, admittedly. I think the parties agreed that we, of course, have to come back to Mr. Inayat once again, and then it's for the parties, the OTP has the burden of proof, no doubt, to identify where a document has been found. And I think it's in agreement that we postponed this -- the completion of the hearing of Mr. Inayat, and we have to come back to this. But from the point of view of a son where the father has worked on the development of the European telex system, I would warn the parties to go into details where this document comes from and where it was sent to. It's very easy to identify this by a witness within one hour, expert witness. So may we please proceed on this basis knowing that we have to come back to the origins of this document with the assistance of Mr. Inayat. This document is admitted into evidence as S150A in the English version, S150B, only the long piece of paper, the telex we have just seen in B/C/S. So please proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I was going to give Mr. Sejmenovic the original. But it's probably easier -- I don't want the registry to swipe it -- so could he be given, please, the B/C/S copy of the number 239, now 150B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, we started to look at this document yesterday. This is apparently a decision of the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region, which has been forwarded to an SJB, to put it neutrally, apparently by Stojan Zupljanin. It states that "only women, children, and the elderly may be moved from the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina if they so wish. Two, the above-mentioned activities shall be carried out in cooperation with humanitarian organisations; three, this decision comes into effect on the day it is passed." And then it states: "For the purposes of implementing the above decision, it is necessary that the staff of your SJB be informed of the contents of the decision and realise the necessary cooperation with humanitarian organisations in your territory." Now, can I just ask, from what you saw of -- and you described to us the movement of women and children -- was this being done, first of all, in cooperation with humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who were not children, women, and the elderly, what were the police doing as far as they were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as they are concerned, they -- it was the police who took them to the camp, the Trnopolje camp. Initially, only women and children were evacuated or transported, escorted exclusively by the military, with no intervention whatsoever by the police or any humanitarian organisation. They did not have any freedom of will, these women and children, as far as that is concerned. They were simply taken to Trnopolje, and sometimes from Trnopolje, they would be taken further on by the train from the local railway station. They also transported these women and children by buses and trucks. Later on, they started trading with people, men, those who had enough money could pay to be taken out. Later on, there was a lot of talk about the Red Cross in Trnopolje, that they would come to Trnopolje, and they would organise the evacuation of all the people who happened to be in the Trnopolje camp at the time. I have to emphasise that this was preceded by a number of transports of women and children from various areas of the Prijedor Municipality to Trnopolje. There were such transports coming from Rizvanovici, Hambarine, Puharska. Part of the population, who temporarily took shelter into the houses of either their children or relatives, were evicted from these houses and sent to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. You can hand the document back, and I want to go back to where we left off yesterday. You were telling us yesterday, Mr. Sejmenovic, how you were at the Prijedor Police Station, the SUP, and you were beaten whilst you were being -- in an office, and then beaten again outside your cell. You told us yesterday that outside your prison cell, "they really beat me black and blue. I could not even stand up for a while afterwards, and then they threw my body into the cell." Can I ask, first of all, how many people were beating you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I was able to see, apart from Dragan Saponja whom I mentioned, that three or four other soldiers were approaching. They had come out from an adjacent room, a very large room, from which I could see some military bunkbeds. Several soldiers ran out of this room, and as far as I can recall, there were three or four of them. I know that they were later joined by several more, and it was a very cramped space. I remember that at one point in time, one soldier accidentally hit another soldier. But at one point I lost consciousness, so I don't know what was going on all the time. I don't know whether other soldiers came later on. All I remember was that I was thrown into the cell afterwards. So apart from Saponja, there were three or four other soldiers. I'm sure about five of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they -- what were they using to beat you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the cell, they hit me and kicked me, and they stomped over my body later on. I remember also one soldier putting the blade of his knife against my neck. He did not cut me, he moved it away. But they continued beating me and kicking me while I was down on the floor. It lasted approximately five or six minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were placed in the cell. And were you left there overnight?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not returned to the cell on that occasion. I was thrown into the cell for the first time. After I had been interrogated in one of the offices, I received these blows outside the cell. And after the beating, they threw me into the cell. And this was the first time that I was in this cell. I spent the night, the following night in the cell, and the following morning until noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I think there must have been an error in the translation, Mr. Sejmenovic, because I didn't say returned. However, okay. So you were there until noon the next day. And then were you taken out of the cell?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was taken out of the cell through a corridor in the SUP building and taken outside the building into a yard where there was a bus waiting. And they -- I was driven on that bus. I later on realised that we were on the way to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before you got on to the bus, did you see anybody that you knew?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several police officers whom I had known before the war and who happened to be in the yard and further on outside the building. But apart from them, I saw Mr. Simo Miskovic outside the building. He was wearing a military camouflage uniform, and he passed by me. I hoped that -- I was hoping that he would see me. I looked him straight in the eye, and I hoped -- I was hoping that I would have an opportunity to explain myself, that he would ask me something, and that I would be able to tell him that I had -- that I hadn't done anything wrong. But he simply turned his head away and continued on his way to the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So then were you taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once at Omarska, were you taken into what appeared to be an administration building?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we got off the bus, I was escorted alongside a group of men who were kneeling down and taken to the administration building where a soldier asked me my personal data, my place and date of birth and some other basic information. This didn't take very long. When he finished taking down my data, two soldiers took me out of the administration building and then took me to a small house and we crossed the asphalt pista on the way to the house. Later on, I learned that this house was commonly referred to by the detainees by the "white house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you in a moment to look at some photographs. But first I should have asked you this: The bus that took you from the SUP to Omarska, can you remember what type of bus it was? Did it have any name or anything?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a regular civilian bus which we used to ride before the war. What I was able to see inside the bus, however, was quite strange to me. Half of the passengers were women and -- young women who were prettily made up, and four or five soldiers who were sitting on various seats on the bus, and an elderly gentleman who kept turning around and looking at me. So at first, I thought that it was a local bus belonging to a company, that it was taking the employees of that company to work. But when we turned to Omarska, when we left the Banja Luka/Prijedor Road, I realised that these people were members of the camp personnel, that they were working in the camp and that the men were investigators and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know -- all I want to know, Mr. Sejmenovic, do you know the name of the company to which the bus belonged?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe its name was Autotransport Prijedor. Actually, there was only one bus company in Prijedor. We referred to it as public transport, public transportation company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you, please, to have a look at a couple of photographs, or maybe just one for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, this one has already been admitted as S15-16. It has got the number 0100-2444. And if that could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just indicate to us, can you see there the building that you first went into, what you call the administration building?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think this building here is the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then you said you were taken from there, after you'd been booked in, as it were, to what was called the white house. Can we see that? Maybe you need to look at another photograph to see it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's quite clear there.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I don't need any others. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Once you were in the white house, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After being beaten again, I was taken from the white house back to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You say after you were beaten again -- once you got into the white house, you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First a civilian came in, a person who was not wearing a military uniform. He abused me verbally. I was alone for about five minutes in the room, and no one came in. But after about five minutes, this civilian came in, and after abusing me verbally, started to beat me. This lasted for a short while. Then this person left the white house and a soldier came in. After that soldier, after the soldier had finished, another soldier came in, and then this exchange of soldiers lasted for some time. The fifth soldier and last who came in also beat me. I was bleeding, and they called an old man over from somewhere to wipe my face. The old man did so, and then two soldiers took me out of the white house and back to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two further questions about that: The first man that came in, a civilian, had you ever seen him before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never before. But I did see him immediately after that, late in that day and over the following days, I did see him several times. We slept there. He was also a camp inmate. And he slept next to me, next to where I slept. His name was -- his nickname was Besa, and his last name was Besic. He was one of the camp inmates who had special arrangements with the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand -- did you later come to understand why it was this man had suddenly come in attacked you, a fellow -- somebody who was a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In an indirect way, Inspector Radakovic, who interrogated me, told me right at the beginning of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His first question after I had been brought in was whether they had beaten me. I said I wasn't sure what was the best thing to say, that they did or that they didn't. And he looked at me and he said: "Of course they did. It's obvious. You're bleeding." And then I said: "What can I say? They did." And then he stated: "Your own man beat you, didn't he?" I said I didn't remember because I was unconscious, so I couldn't remember who it was that had beaten me. Later on, when he ordered for me to be taken to the building referred to as the "glass house," at some point in the afternoon, this civilian who had beaten me in the white house came in. I noticed that he was trying to sit down next to me. I thought he would start beating me again. However, he just asked me whether they had beaten me. And I said they did. And he asked me: "Do you know who it was?" And I said: "Well, I'm not sure. There were many of them." Thereupon he said: "It's all right." The whole thing began to dawn on me at that point, but I knew it was his task to do what he had done, and it was clear he was checking whether I could remember that he had beaten me and whether I would later at some point blame him for that. I answered by letting him know, by making him believe that I could not remember whether he was the man who took part in the beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the only other thing, then, is this: Whilst this beating was going on, that is, by the soldiers, the military, was anybody saying anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept saying things, abusive remarks. Saying that I had spoken out against the Serb army, the Serb assembly, that I was an extreme extremist, fundamentalist, that I ended up exactly where I was meant to end up. And a number of other abusive remarks concerning also my looks, and I know that when I was taken out of the white house, several soldiers came running my way with the intention of hitting me. But the policemen who were escorting me told them not to touch me while the questioning was still underway and later each and "every one of us would take our turn." I heard this, and that's literally what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've told us that you were interrogated by somebody called Radakovic. Had you come across him before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had. Even before the war. He was the director of the national park of Kozara. He had an MA in psychology, and he was also a painter. He had graduated from an art academy. He was an elderly gentleman. I heard from the camp inmates that those who had been questioned by Mr. Radakovic were those who were the worst off, and that most people succumbed in the cell where he interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What was he -- briefly, if you can, in summary, what was he interrogating you about?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questioning took off in the following way: The first thing he said: "Look, Sejmenovic, we're not into weapons. We're not interested in weapons. We know that you didn't have any weapons. There was a very small amount of weapons, peanuts," as he said, "but that doesn't matter. What we're really after is Sarajevo. The functioning of the government, the relationships within the government," and then these sessions of questioning went on for several days. What he most insisted on was for me to tell him about Miomir Simovic and Vitomir Zepinic the two Serbs who had remained loyal to Bosnia-Herzegovina and who had agreed to become members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government during that period, or immediately following the Serb separation. They wanted me to tell them all the details about seeing Simovic and Zepinic whether anyone had said anyone. They asked questions about Fikret Abdic also, and to a lesser extent about the SDA officials in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said this interrogation went on for several days. Where were you kept in between interrogations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a room that was referred to as the "glass house." Soldiers would not come into this room to beat the camp inmates, at least not during the period that I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to just ask you again to look, if you can see the building which the glass house was in that photograph you've already looked at. If not, we'll show you another photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's S15-16.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. The glass house was a building here. It was at the junction point between these two buildings, and there is a space in between that is built in glass and not roofed over. So this is the area we used to refer to as the "glass house." I'm pointing at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think when we look at the video, we'll be able to see what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you can take the photograph away. Thank you very much, usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were kept in the glass house, and you said soldiers would not come into this room to beat the camp inmates while you were in there. Was there a special class of inmate in that glass house area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that staying in the glass house meant that you would not be beaten during the day or at night. Many times, guards would come over to the door of the glass house and abuse me verbally, said things about my mother, about my relatives, about the state, and they said that someday I'd be out of the glass house at last, which was a sign for me that actually they were forbidden to enter the glass house. In the glass house, I saw a number of people, some of whom were members of the 5th Kozarac Brigade, who had responded to the mobilisation and who had fought against the Serbs in Croatia, who had fought with the Serbs in Croatia. They were also arrested regardless of their loyalty and taken to Omarska, but some of them, as a token of gratitude from the Serbs for having taken part in their struggle, were placed in the glass house in order to be spared the beatings. I also saw a number of people there who had been very badly beaten, in the period just preceding their transfer to the glass house. I saw a man there who had worked for the SUP station in Prijedor, the public security station. He had been beaten black and blue, head to waist. It was as though he had been tattooed in bruises, and he spent several days in one of the hangars there before someone managed to get him transferred to the glass house. And he arrived there in the shape which I have just described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody ever explain why it was that you, who were in the glass house, were not being beaten despite attempts for soldiers to enter, or guards, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not during the questioning, nor when Mr. Radakovic ordered them to put me in the glass house. He never told me why. Excuse me, it's important to add another thing. I also heard that some people had paid a lot of money to be put in the glass house and to be transferred there from the other hangars. What I saw with my own eyes was Mr. Hilmija Nukic who lived on the border line between Trnopolje and the village of Hrnici. I had known him before the war and he had served in the Serb army until August 1992. I saw him in the glass house, and I saw him take out of his pocket the last golden chain he had on him and he saw him give it to a Serb soldier or guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there some a time when some foreign journalists and indeed Serb journalists came to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, Serb soldiers began to arrive. Mr. Mutic came on the fifth day of the questioning, and then soldiers came to take me again to Mr. Radakovic's office, but they didn't come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you just pause. Did you hear the question, Mr. Sejmenovic? Because I'm not sure it was translated. I asked you about foreign journalists and Serb journalists.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. The witness did say journalists. I'm sorry, it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was a mistake in the interpretation. Right. All right. Should the answer have been - perhaps it should be translated back - that at first Serb journalists began to arrive. Mr. Mutic came on the fifth day of the questioning and then soldiers or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, the best thing is I'll start the whole questioning again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I'm sorry. Mr. Sejmenovic, Serb journalists came to the camp, did they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that after you had been there for some five days?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first time was on the fifth day, approximately, and the second time was, I think, on the seventh day. So Mutic came and then reappeared after two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who was Mr. Mutic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a local journalist for Kozarski Vjesnik. He also collaborated on Radio Prijedor, and he showed up with a camera and with a text that I was supposed to read into the camera. I had known him and he had known me before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to watch a film in a moment. But how many times altogether were you interviewed by journalists?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three times. After Mutic, foreign journalists arrived in Omarska. And the same day after they had refused to talk to me, I was taken to a room to which Dragan Bozanic came, a journalist from the Serbian television, and asked me several questions to which I replied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what we're going to look at in a moment, but before we do that, you say that Mr. Mutic came armed with a camera and a text that you were supposed to read into the camera. What was the text that he wanted you to read?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a text stating who was to blame for the war. Names of extremists were given in the text who had prepared the attack on the Serbian people. There were several sentences about the Muslim priests arming their believers, and that everything happened under the aegis of the SDA through which Alija Izetbegovic was planning to establish a Muslim state. I know that several local names were dropped there. He told me that my fate, whether I would remain alive, would very much depend on what I did. He told me to read the text and that he would then ask me questions on the basis of that text. And that, he said, would save my life because it was being reported -- recorded, and the Red Cross would see that I was alive in Omarska, so they would then not kill me. That was when he first came. He said he would return. And the second time, when he returned, he brought the text I'm talking about. It was then he came with a camera and recorded me reading the text and then retelling it. It was only two days after that that I noticed some sort of a strange atmosphere in the camp. After two, it was clear that something was happening. And then a huge number of foreign journalists thronged into the camp. And while they were still there at the administration building, I was taken to a floor and asked those questions. Mr. Bozanic told me that he would be back to make a special programme with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This is what I want to have a look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we play the video, there is a transcript available. Your Honour, the transcript is in English. There is, however, a Bosnian version. I'm wondering what the best way of dealing with this is for the interpreters using the Bosnian transcript to interpret. I don't know whether Your Honours' colleague would be able to follow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, was the English and the B/C/S version disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it's available for us in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a transcript, yes, in English. I don't think a B/C/S version is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll hear, of course, the text in B/C/S. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you'll hear -- no, it will all be in B/C/S, although you can hear, because it's the Serb television crew following the ITN television crew for the first bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's the most adequate solution to give us the English version and then it's, of course, for the Defence to contest whether or not it's correct on the basis of the entire video, if necessary. Right? Proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I hand out ... And if somebody could turn Mr. Sejmenovic's screen on to the video. He can probably do it himself. Yes, if we could play the video, then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Prijedor looks rather gloomy after the fierce clashes between the Muslim and the Serbian units. Many villages are almost completely burned down, the houses demolished. At the time of the census, Muslims and Serbs lived in this municipality in roughly even numbers, and in this war, after days of bloody battles, Serbian units control almost the entire area of the municipality. A press briefing was held first thing today in Prijedor at which the Minister of Information in the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Velibor Ostojic, briefly stated: "In Prijedor, as is the case on the entire territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, nobody's concealing anything." And then he asked the reporters to visit the territory controlled by the Muslim and Croatian units all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. The mayor of Prijedor, Milomir Stakic, in the mine or, rather, in the administration building of this mine Omarska, there is an investigation centre, and in the village of Trnopolje, there is a reception centre where 4.500 people have found shelter. Most of them want to move out of this area, the majority of those to the north-west, that is to Croatia, Slovenia, and Western European countries. "The Serbs here are willing to live together with everyone who does not have blood on their hands," said Mayor Stakic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could we please have for the interpretation a break, if possible, after one paragraph. Otherwise, the French booth, I'm afraid, can't follow this pace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- of course, it's the commentator on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the person responsible for the video has one copy of the English version available, and then stop immediately after one paragraph, it would be excellent and facilitate the work of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Next comes to a visit to Omarska. Here there are 175 people, rather malnourished, and their guards. They agreed to talk to journalists, and asked for cigarettes. We have rather extensive audio recordings of all this and we shall broadcast it in the days to come. More than 3.000 people have gone through this investigation centre, the investigators say. They produce lists and evidence that most of them were organised on a military basis. There are 175 of them here at the moment. We go to Trnopolje next. In the local school and its yard there are roughly 4.500 people who are free to leave the area but are reluctant to do so. Only one older man has died in this collection centre since 28 May, they say. The Red Cross department complains that there is not enough food. The majority, and we talked with them without any hindrance, want to emigrate to the northwest. They do not want to go towards Sarajevo. Finally, we should say that military sources, or more precisely Colonel Vladimir Arsic expressly told the press that the army had nothing to do with this collection centre in Trnopolje and the investigation centre in Omarska. These are under the sole jurisdiction of the municipality civilian authorities, and it is our impression that these authorities are not up to dealing with the turmoil of war and in this particular case, the regional authorities of the Bosnian Krajina have also failed to act."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "the first group of reporters that was given such a permission by the presidency of Republika Srpska included reporters of the two channels of the British independent TV network ITN and The Guardian journalist. They were accompanied by our TV crew. All the material we have filmed was taped in the same places where our foreign colleagues turned on their cameras. We must remark that our camera also recorded in those same places things that might shed more light on the alleged harassment of civilians in the camps as they say, or investigative centres, as representatives of Serb authorities stress."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop, please. Our English translation starts earlier, one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just saying the same thing to Ms. Sutherland. I wondered what happened to the first paragraph. It was the voiceover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could we please restart clip 2 from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The first group of reporters that was given such a permission by the presidency of the Republika--"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pause for a moment. Your Honour, I don't know. Can I say that this transcript was provided so long ago at the Tadic trial -- What? Oh sorry. I'm corrected by Ms. Sutherland, who is the historian -- the Kovacevic trial, and it may well be that there are a number of different copies of the same version. And it may well be that this is another one. I think it may be better just to exclude that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, if we could carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "ITN and The Guardian journalist, they were accompanied by our TV crew. All the material that we have filmed was taped in the same places where our foreign colleagues turned on their cameras. We must remark that our camera also recorded, in those same places, things that might shed more light, on the alleged harassment of civilians in the camps, as they say, or investigative centres, as the representatives of Serb authorities stress." "We need to stress right away that we immediately realised that our British colleagues came with orders to film concentration camps in Serb territory. One can call a certain institution a concentration camp only in the respect of the definition given by international law. Foreign reporters showed no interest for facts, for example, that they would be travelling along the recently established corridor that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Pause and go back for a moment, please. Yes. Yes. And then just forward slightly until we see that house which I think we've now lost. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, it's not terribly clear, but can you tell us what road were the reporters travelling along?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were moving from the direction of Prijedor towards Omarska. This portion here is the area of Kamicani or Jakupovici. It was on that section of the road. One can see that the houses there had been destroyed. It was then that the majority of the houses were destroyed. Actually, most of the houses had already been destroyed, those located alongside the road. Some of them were destroyed then, and some later on, when tanks were used to raze them to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just tell us the villages that you mentioned, that is, Kamicani and Jakupovici --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this looks like Donja Jakupovici, or perhaps a portion of the village of Zecovi or the village of Hadzici. But most probably it is the village of Donja Jakupovici which is next to the road in question. Gornji Jakupovici is situated on the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just confirm, what ethnicity composed the population of these villages? Terrible sentence.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All non-Serbs. If I may add one further point, generally speaking as regards this footage, an identical footage would be if they took the road from Kozarac to Prijedor, the area of Mujkanovici for example, and further on towards Trnopolje. These scenes could be seen everywhere in all of the non-Serbs areas, except for a small portion of the Trnopolje area where there was a number of houses which were not burned down or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can go on with the film.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Along the recently established corridor that has vital importance for the Republika Srpska. Even though during our trip it was shelled from Croatia by ZNG troops. They also did not ask who destroyed and set fire to villages and towns we passed through, who attacked the very centre of Prijedor just a few days earlier, who had built and equipped with arms underground bunkers on Mount Kozara, nor did they wonder why Muslim women are allowed to visit freely their husbands and sons in the localities we were taking them to, the investigative, that is, reception centre, in Omarska and Trnopolje near Prijedor. After the almost completely normal situation in and around Prijedor and Banja Luka, the shooting in the vicinity of the management building of the Omarska mine reminded of the presence of a number of Muslim extremists and terrorists groups in the area around Ljubija."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pause for a moment there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, Mr. Sejmenovic, what the camera is showing us now.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago we saw the building where the restaurant was, that is, where people from time to time took meals and where they sometimes slept during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the building that we're looking at now, that's the building with the restaurant in it.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's all one entire area, that is, the restaurant, the offices, and the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think maybe the best thing to do Mr. Sejmenovic if there's anything you want to say, if you can just say "stop" and they will stop the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we can carry on, please. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Now, here we can see Dragan Bozanic, a journalist from the Srna television, a Serb television who did the interview that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he's the one closest to the camera with the short-sleeved shirt, is he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I think that that's him. The image is not very good, but a moment ago, as we were watching the film, I think I recognise -- I was able to recognise Dragan Bozanic. We can move on. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We arrived in Omarska" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop here. Here we see the detainees in the restaurant taking their meal. What is perhaps -- what might be useful for the purposes of having a better insight into the overall situation, maybe I should give some further explanation regarding the atmosphere at that time. Unlike several previous days, during which the soldiers and guards in the mine were wearing soiled clothes, dirty clothes, dirty uniforms, and carrying their weapons cocked, on that day, they arrived in perfectly clean uniforms. Some of them were even wearing new uniforms. And we noticed that they were carrying their rifles like this. But we heard very loud shooting in the immediate vicinity of the camp. We didn't know what was going on. But when the first groups of detainees were taken in to have their meal, they were told to eat very slowly. Otherwise, normally they were always told to finish as quickly as possible. We only had 30 or 60 seconds to sit down and eat the meal. And we had to run back regardless of whether we had finished or not. When this group of detainees entered the restaurant, the guards ordered that everyone should eat slowly, and this is what you can see on this footage. You can see people eating at an almost normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We can carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The mine has not been operational for quite some time, but the restaurant is normally functional. No aid and food and other items needed in this investigative centre managed by the civilian authorities in Prijedor arrived from any foreign party, including the Red Cross, even though large sums are needed for food only. "The Omarska centre holds mostly those individuals who took active part in military operations. In Trnopolje, several kilometres away, the premises are used for others, a total of about 3400 men. "Mr. Simo Drljaca, superintendent of the Prijedor public security department in Prijedor, is explaining -- is providing explanation to the foreign journalists."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just pause for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, Simo Drljaca that we see there talking to the foreign journalists, had you seen him at the camp before that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not, not before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually know Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was with the police. I saw him several times on various occasions, but I didn't have any direct contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can go on. Can we go on, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The third category are those who threw away their weapons and now it is difficult to prove they actually had one. You understand. They got rid of the rifle, and now it's difficult to prove that he was ever armed. "Would you be so kind and tell us what's happening. While we're speaking, we heard shots. "Look here, this is not safe territory. Part of the extremists are spread along there. Those are all Muslim villages back there." "You haven't answered my question. "A few kilometres in that direction are Muslim villages. There are still some extremists there active. They operate in groups of about a dozen. They come out from their dugouts and attack. Here we have a large number of men. "British reporters did not want to visit the infirmary in the centre, nor were they interested to meet prisoner Mevludin Sejmenovic, member of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina and SDA activist in the zone. "We have heard that you are one of nine rare inhabitants of this reception centre who came to Omarska on his own. "Yes, that's correct. "Can you explain to us why you did that, why did you come here? "I spent some time waiting and hiding. I waited for all the prime actors in these horrendous events to be captured, for the truth to be established about what has happened, about the people that have done all the evil so that my efforts and my work, as well as the statements that I am going to give, can be appreciated. "When you say "captured", who exactly do you have in mind? Who do you think responsible for the atrocities that have taken place here? "Well, I'm referring first of all to the party leader of Bosanska Krajina, Mirza Mujadzic, and the chairman of the Prijedor party branch, and a member of the party executive council for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm also referring to the men working in -- for the party and those who have organised these military activities. "Your fellow colleagues in this centre, do they know about your opinion? Do they share your views about the evil that struck the Muslim people? "I have spoken about that on two occasions: When we had discussions here, in an interview for the Krajina TV as well. I have made a statement and addressed a message to my people concerning the whole situation which I am now able to witness directly here in Bosnian Krajina and in Prijedor, which is not -- which is not theoretically like those who are watching it from a distance and who are the masterminds of this evil. "I don't know whether you're aware of the fact that some foreign journalists, mostly Great Britian, have also come to visit this centre. The reason for this visit is the fact that over the past few days, international media have been affirming that in the Republika Srpska, that is the territory where you are now, there are concentration camps for Muslims and Croats. You are in this particular centre, and you have come on your own. Could you tell these foreign reporters what the truth is. Do you know what is actually a concentration camp? What is your -- what would be your message to them? "I would like them to know that the military operations have caused -- have brought about such effects that it became necessary for people to group up, both for reasons of safety and for mere survival. This centre is not a concentration camp in the sense affirmed by political propaganda, and I think that today they were able to see it for themselves. "One last question: Before the flames of war started here, were there any Muslims living in the area who were actually getting ready for war? "Over the past few months, there was a lot of talk about these arms and weapons, even amongst the ordinary people, but also amongst the members of political parties, including the SDA. There was a lot of fear and insecurity, and people were searching for some form of stronghold, at least, by talking about personal safety. However, it is now perfectly clear that political oligarchies were involved in shady deals operating behind the back of the party members and the ordinary people. Their objective was to have people fight for their private or individual interests, without taking into account the real consequences that will inevitably follow such actions. "Even foreigners are now able to to conclude that this war has all the characteristics of a religious war. Have you heard of any Muslim priests, hodzas, and imams having any special American hunting rifles which they had prepared before the war? "I know very little about weapons and the ways to procure them. There were lots of talks about that. There is ample evidence to this effect. Still, bearing in mind talks with ordinary people, there is evidence that a certain number of priests were involved in arms smuggling or some other form of procurement of weapons. I only know that by doing so, they have breached both the norms and rules of the religions. They preach, and human moral norms [as interpreted]. They, too, have merits for all this evil that has fallen upon all the peoples living here. "The centre in Trnopolje, as we have indicated, is only a few kilometres away from Omarska. Security is far more relaxed than in Omarska, and the centre has been set up for those in respect of whom it could not be established that they opposed the Serb authorities. With the help of UNPROFOR, or through the all for all prisoner exchange arrangements, they are able to leave the centre. However, until now neither Sarajevo nor UNPROFOR reacted to this option. I think that we can and we must go on living as we did before, so there is no other solution. We are innocent. We are civilians. We are not guilty of anything. Those over there want some sort of Eastern Bosnia. Here they are talking about a Western Bosnia. I don't know all this talk about independent states. It's impossible. Look at my neighbour here. I've known him for 25 years. And today he is on one side and I am on the other. "A lot of blood has been shed between two peoples can life in common, coexistence be re-established? "Here in Prijedor yes it can. Nothing too bad happened." "What government are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But even with the transcript it is impossible to interpret because the speakers are constantly overlapping. I'm sorry, I cannot hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we break. Apparently, there is a problem with the booth. It's totally understandable that it's impossible. We can only read out this and follow it by reading it ourselves. But it's necessary to have a break here and there. And possibly on the basis of the English version, we may have access to the French as well, if it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may help. I've let it run on because the transcript's there and it's showing Trnopolje. But the major part that I played this for was obviously for Mr. Sejmenovic to watch himself. I'm perfectly happy to continue or stop. If the Defence want the whole video played through, then we'll do it. Otherwise I'll stop it here, which may make it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do. But if they want to wait, we can bring it in during our cross, whichever --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, we will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it's better to proceed, but I think it's appropriate that we have a break now. And in the meantime, it may be discussed amongst the interpreters themselves how it's the best way to proceed. I think it would be fine if we have the English text before us. We make a break here and there in between in order to have a French translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one other option, which is what I thought might be simpler, which is I think there must be somewhere, and we can make inquiries in the break, a transcript that was -- because in order to translate, somebody had to write out what was heard. And it may be easier from the point of the French if the translator has a B/C/S transcript in front of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's find out during the break how we can proceed in the most appropriate way to give access to all participants here in the courtroom at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 4.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. We made inquiries, but it appears that no transcript in B/C/S was made. It was direct listening to the tape. We're going to resubmit the tape because it has been pointed out to us there are some errors in the translation. But I think -- I regret to say the only way is just to play to the end of the tape now and hope that the interpreters will manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. If we can do it once again portion by portion, and the interpreters please may indicate if it's too fast and a break is needed. So please start.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Who is to blame for it? The blue collars and farmers are not responsible for this state of things. "We have a house, a wife children, we certainly do not want to go to war. This has been forced upon us. "We also filmed the interview conducted by the British reporters, the man was prompted by his fellows and he responded in English. "I think it is very quiet. Nothing wrong. "Mehmed says that everything here is quiet. That nothing bad is happening. "You sleep outside? "No, no, inside. "He says that it is hot, but that they sleep in the school building, not in the open. The British reporter then asks whether they have been maltreated. "No, they have been very kind. "Are you a fighter? "Mehmed says he was not a fighter. "You feel safe here? "He also tells her that he feels quite safe and that except for the heat, everything is all right. "This man is very thin. "The female reporter insisted that one of the men was very thin. And Mehmed explained, not all the people are the same. "Not all the people are the same. He then added that this is not a prison. "If you wanted to get on a bus to Banja Luka, could you do that this afternoon? "I think it depends on the civil government. "We have no idea what was the report presented to the British viewers and the viewers in the rest of the world like. We do know that the foreign crew did not visit the kitchen where food was prepared for them, nor the Red Cross offices, nor the other group of inmates that should not even be called that because they came here seeking shelter and food which they were given. "I think it's not a prison. It's a refugee camp. Simple. "You are a doctor in this reception centre. What is it officially called? "Trnopolje reception centre. "And are you a Muslim? "Yes, and I'm an inmate like the others. "Can you tell us how you feel in the centre, what is lifelike here? "How can a man feel in a camp? It's not very pleasant. "You have a chance of doing a job you have been trained for. Do you have the necessary conditions for it? "No. "There is a shortage of medicines. "We have what we managed to bring along. We have received nothing else. "Is it enough to treat the inmates? "No. Basic medicines, antibiotics for diarrhea are needed, but very scarce. "What about the other medicines? "We have those. We see a long queue of people waiting to see you. Do you have any doubt on the number of individuals medically treated? "Since we've been here, May the 26th, that is, well, since that date, we have registered 5169 persons. Not all have been registered, however. "This entire part of the Republic of Srpska was in a blockade. Economic blockade and shortage of food. Do you think that you have equally shouldered the lack of food, or were you discriminated? "No, it was quite the same. As far as the blockade is concerned, everyone suffers the same. "Did you have any deaths? "Yes. "What was the cause, disease? "Well, we did have one case at the very beginning. It was an old man. He was quite old, and he died of sickness. "He did not die for lack of medicines. "No, he didn't. "I'm asking you this because a large part of Europe did not want to hear about the problem of babies in the Banja Luka maternity hospital when one of them died due to the shortage of oxygen. "There's a health centre here and a hospital and they have major problems due to shortage of antibiotics and diarrhea drugs. It's a problem in the entire area, not only for us here. "Not only in the reception centre? "No, it's not only a problem we face. "Could you tell us your name? "Merscanic Ipriz or Mersalic Idriz. "You have not been long here and you work for the Red Cross. Can you tell us what the situation is? Do you have sufficient supplies to cover your basic activity: Helping those that came to you or that need help? Lamentably, with the aid we have available, we can do very little. We are here from the first day. People from the surrounding area came here, most of them of their own free will. Partial already for lack of food and very often it was because they planned to evacuate or hope to, to central Bosnia. "Practically to escape from the zone where the fighting raged? "Right. To escape the war. There were several evacuations. The first were more sensitive, both on our end and on their side, but as the situation developed, they became voluntary and much less sad. "Since you are with a major international organisation, can you tell us whether you received any aid from the central headquarters or branches in former Yugoslavia or Europe? "No, we did not receiving anything on these grounds. We received only aid for refugees from Croatia. As far as this situation here is concerned, aid that came arrived mostly from Serbia. I really cannot say that international aid helped us here. "So what might be called aid provided by the international Red Cross in war zones did not arrive here? "No. Only Banja Luka granted some aid to Prijedor from what was sent by international organisations, but that was generally intended for refugees of another type. "As far as the refugees in this area are concerned, ever since Prijedor became a combat zone, they do not enjoy the status of refugees, but rather the status of displaced persons. That's the treatment they receive. "We can say that broader aid would be welcome? "Certainly, we need it. At the present moment, we have absolutely no possibility of intervening. None at all. We have extremely modest resources. The secretary of the Red Cross organisation in Prijedor left for Belgrade today to ask for aid. "So help is expected from Serbia, from Yugoslavia? "Mostly from Yugoslavia. "Can anyone tell me something about your status here? Do you enjoy freedom of movement? Can you go away if you want? "They do let us go around the village. We bring back whatever we find. "You mean that this fence is not separating you from the village? "No, they let us go out. We leave our ID card and we can go around a couple of kilometres to the village. "You did not explain. There is no one in the village now. We go around the gardens and pick vegetables and such. "So you freely take a hoe and dig up whatever you find in a vegetable patch? "Yes, we dig up potatoes or whatever. "However, there's little left around to pick now. "Yes, food is getting scarce in the village as well. "When did you come here? "May 27th. "Why did you come here? "I came when the shelling started up there. I had to. Where else could I have gone? "Did you take part in military operations? "No, I didn't. "You came here looking for shelter? "Right. You can see for yourself, it isn't that bad. "Were there any problems, did anyone maltreat you? "No, no one did. "Was anyone here maltreated? In the camp we visited a little while ago there were people that arrived from another reception centre. Is this reception centre a camp where people are harassed? "This is a reception centre. It can't be anything else but a reception centre. Here all those came who did not take part in the fighting. What would they be fighting for then? Those that saw shelling had to come here. "What are you hoping for now? "If someone could line up those bigwigs before a firing squad, we would be living together again. That's what should be done. "I'm from a village nearby. From Kamicani. "Why did you come here? "There was shooting. A war broke out. "Did anyone chase you away from your home, under the threat of arms? "Well, I was lucky, and I came here with little kids, small children. I came from the fields. No one harassed us. They did not harm us. I stayed in the village for two weeks. Then they were sent on. They said, I don't know where. Some of my people reached Zagreb already. Went to Sisak. However, some who had relatives went there, mostly to Croatia. "It's the politics that brought people to this situation. Maybe they had far too good a life, nothing else. "This was a rich zone, fertile lands? "It's not that fertile, but people worked hard. Richness is where you make it. "But one could live a good life here? "You sure could. You could. "As far as you know, would they join Alija Izetbegovic's troops Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 4786 to 4793. again, if you were to release them? "I am certain that all those belonging to the first and second category would immediately join Alija Izetbegovic's troops. However, I'm also certain that those from the third category would not join Alija's jihad. In any case, they will be given the possibility of finding a place to live, either here or somewhere abroad? To be honest, I would like those belonging to the third category to stay and live together with us. "This was a review of the prisoner camps in Serbian-controlled Bosnian Krajina, filmed by our crew. Foreign reporters are still rushing to Omarska and Trnopolje. Will they also visit the prisons run by Izetbegovic's democratic authorities? Will they be given permission, like they have been in the Republika Srpska? Lamentably, this is a question that the Republika Srpska television cannot answer. Along the main road representing the vital artery of the Bosnian and Knin Krajina, there are many house in ruins. Were they owned by Muslims, Croats, or maybe Serbs?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we -- Let's just finish the clip, then. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you very much. You can stop it. Well, Your Honour, I say that. This video contains a number of clips, but they are later and they are not relevant as far as I'm aware. But again, if I could ask my learned friends of the Defence whether they want the remainder of the video played.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, first of all, when the cameras panned around during the time that you were actually being interviewed, we were able to see you sitting in what appeared to be a glass-type of corridor. Is that what you're calling the glass house area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back and ask you, in a little more detail, about this particular interview. You've told us that Mr. Bozanic came and said that you would be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you the chronology of the events on that day. So immediately before the interview and the course of the interview itself. When foreign journalists recorded this footage in the restaurant, they left the restaurant. About half an hour later, two guards came over to the glass house and called me to stand up and come with them immediately. One of the guards said to the other persons who were in the glass house: "Give him a white shirt" and he ordered an older gentleman who was wearing a white shirt to take it off and give it to me. I found out that the shirt was too big for me, and I was hesitant to take off the shirt I was wearing. The guard told me: "Hurry up. We don't have much time." Eventually he told me to come with them, and I went in wearing the shirt that I was wearing before. They took me out of the glass house, through the corridor, and up to the first floor of the administration building. In the corridor, on the first floor, as I climbed up, I saw there a group of foreign journalists, Serb officers, and a blond woman I recognised in this footage. She was an interpreter. We stopped in front of them, and one of the foreign journalists asked her, and she translated it for me. They refused to talk to me. After that, the guards took me further down the corridor to a large room where they put me up, and I was let there alone for several minutes. After a couple of minutes, Dragan Bozanic entered the room with the cameraman and several guards at the same time. He said: "Mr. Sejmenovic, we shall now do the interview. Light a cigarette if you like, before we begin." I refused, but they said that I should feel free to light one and that they wouldn't start recording yet, as I was in no position to refuse, I lit a cigarette. He took the microphone, the camera was turned on, and then he started asking me questions as we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given, before the interview, any kind of text or given any instructions as to what you should say?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to this interview, immediately before the interview, no. But I had been prepared in the days preceding the interview when I talked to Mutic, the other journalist, and I gathered that the same sort of principle would be applied again for the other interview, that my own behaviour decreased or increased my chances of survival. In essence, I knew what it was they wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to ask you about some of the things that you said. You were asked by the journalist --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the third page of the transcript, fourth page, I'm sorry. The question where it says it's from the journalist off camera, and then "man."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was put to you by the journalist that you had come to Omarska on your own, and you said: "Yes, that's correct." "Can you explain why you did that, why did you come here?" "I came here after waiting and hiding around for some time" et cetera. You told us that, in fact, you had been taken to Omarska from the police station. Why did you say that to the reporter?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to say it like that, under those circumstances because that was a matter of life and death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel that you were able to say to the Serb -- Bosnian Serb reporter that you had, in fact, been arrested and beaten up at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was by no means in a position to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the reporter asked you: "Who is responsible for the horrors that have taken place in this zone?" And you replied: "First of all, I have in mind the party leader for Bosnian Krajina, Mirza Mujadzic, and chairman of the party branch in Prijedor, also Mirza Mujadzic." Why were you blaming Mr. Mujadzic for the horrors that had taken place in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to do it. Bozanic and the journalists before him wanted to have just that kind of statement. What I tried to avoid, by all means, was to mention the names of people who were in the camp or might be in the camp or might have been in the camp. In answering their questions, I was, in a manner of speaking, buying time, so I started talking about the functions and positions that Mr. Mujadzic was holding in order to just prolong my answer and avoid mentioning a number of other names. I dropped his name first because I had learned that he was alive and that he had already reached the free territory in the Bihac zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, blame Mr. Mujadzic for what had happened in the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, by no means. That was never my opinion, and the facts show quite the opposite. But it is very important that Bozanic came to Omarska, made an interview with me, and wanted to produce a piece of propaganda to defend their policy. This was actually military or political propaganda, a piece of military or political propaganda, this footage that was recorded. I was quite aware of that, and I tried to behave in such a way so as to put no one's life at risk because of my answer, but also, as far as I could, to satisfy the expectations of Mr. Bozanic and to buy myself some time, too, a day or two. It was very difficult in such a short time to find an appropriate answer to reconcile all these demands and save my own life. I tried to provide abstract answers, to the extent that I could, without specifying anything. And in part, at least I believe, I succeeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just look at a couple of other things that you said. The reporter -- you explained that you had already been interviewed before, but the reporter then asked you whether this was a concentration camp or a reception centre. And you talked about military operations, meaning that people had to group for reasons of safety and survival. And then said: "This centre is not a concentration camp in the sense affirmed by political propaganda." Would you, from your admittedly limited stay in Omarska, have described it as a reception centre?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was definitely a concentration camp with no rules, with no due course of justice. People were killed for no reason at all. People were accused and tried sometimes for things they had nothing to do with. There were minors. I myself saw a child, 16 years of age, whose both arms were broken above the elbows. They forced him to sing Serbian songs for two days. He was tortured in an office which was opposite the office in which I was being questioned. I later watched this child. He couldn't eat, and two elderly men took him out of the room holding him by his arms in the air, tried to feed him with spoons. And this went on for a while. I'm not sure whether he survived. There was absolutely no element there involved, resembling anything remotely like a reception centre there. People who were there knew this clearly. The interview, I tried to provide abstract answers, as I said. But foreign journalists could see everything for themselves. My line of thinking was: "If I survive, that is clear, the eyewitnesses were there. And then my position was also quite clear. I was one of the inmates. They wanted to use me politically for their own propaganda. I knew that my life depended on my actions. It had been suggested to me, this possibility, by a soldier a couple of days before who escorted me in a car to the police station in Prijedor. His name was Banovic. And at one point, as I've said earlier in my testimony, he asked me an intimate question. I saw my chance there, because he was asking me about something that had nothing to do with the war, to ask him a question about my own fate. And I did. And then he answered in a way that was later -- that later proved very helpful. I asked him whether they would kill me immediately or later, what the procedure was. And he told me: "It doesn't necessarily mean that they will kill you." I'm quoting Mr. Banovic here. "It all depends on what sort of answers you provide." I kept asking: "What would be the best thing for me to tell them?" He said: "I have no idea. May God be with you." That's how our conversation ended. And the sentence remained with me in the back of my mind for days afterwards, that sentence and what Mutic, the journalist, had told me, that my life, whether I live or die, depended on what I would say. Your Honours, I have recounted this to you now in order to help you to understand the context in which I was made to answer those questions. That was why I confirmed that I had been come to Omarska of my own free will, that's why I was introduced by Bozanic as someone who was just there for a visit. Of course, I wasn't. It would have been mad for me at that point to say that I was actually not there for just a visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, then, about one final thing that you were asked about. You said -- you were asked, rather, were there any among the Muslims who had prepared for war. And you said: "It is now definitively clear that political oligarchies were involved in turbid affairs operating behind the back of the party members and the ordinary people. Their goal was to make the people fight for their private and individual interests, without taking into account the real effects that inevitably follow such actions." Did you genuinely believe that there were people, political oligarchies operating behind the party members and ordinary people, effectively inciting people to fight, the Muslims to fight?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I used the expression "political oligarchies" in plural, not a political oligarchy, which would mean the SDA, but oligarchies. The reason I said that was because I was also counting on the possibility for this interview to be viewed elsewhere in the world, and also in the free territory. I did not wish to pronounce the sentences which would have branded me as a Serb collaborator. And that was the reason why I endeavoured to the extent it was possible to use these abstract sentences, and I remember using the expression "political oligarchies," though it is a pure abstraction. Had he asked me about my arguments for that, I don't think I would be able to give him an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, and this is the next page of the transcript, Mr. Sejmenovic, you were asked whether you had heard that some Muslim priest, hodzas, and imams had special American hunting rifles. And you said that there is evidence that a certain number of priests were involved in arms smuggling or some other form of procurement of weapons. Had you heard about hodzas or imams being involved in arms smuggling?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I had not heard about that. I did not have any evidence for that.
