But I know that one of the elements of the Serb propaganda even before the war was the argument that Muslim priests had taken part in the arming of the population, that they had been preparing for a Muslim war against Serbs and so on and so forth. There were many similar arguments made. In this interview, and even in the previous one to Mr. Mutic, it was clear to me that they wanted to hear something about the priests from the detainees themselves. They wanted to elicit this type of statements. I was forced to provide an answer to the question that had been asked. And once again, I tried not to be specific, and I believe that that satisfied Mr. Bozanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. That's all I want to ask you about that interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask for the admission of the video and transcript into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I first of all ask, is there any 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it available for the Chamber, a copy of this video?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your own copy? I'm not sure. We can get a copy made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence has a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it's your intention, if I understand correctly, to tender the video itself and the English translation as regards Clip 1, Clip 2, without the first paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just perhaps a point of clarification, Your Honour, it was my understanding that we'll add the English translation of these respective clips as a draft translations because I think the counsel suggested that they were going to resend it for better or for clearer translation because there were some, respectfully, errors or mistakes that were seen on the face of it from the interpretation provided this afternoon by our interpreters here and that which is contained in the text. So with that provision, we have no other objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do confirm that we will -- what we do is replace what is what we will call this draft translation with a new translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, the video as such is admitted into evidence as S151. The draft translation of Clip 1 and Clip 2, without the first paragraph to be read on page 2, is admitted into evidence as S151A. And it should be added to the list of exhibits that a draft and rough interpretation of this video can be found on today's transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to come to how you were able to leave Omarska. The following day, did another television crew arrive?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the following day, no television crew arrived the next day, at least I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, that will teach me to lead on the transcript. Mr. Sejmenovic, can you tell us -- can you remember how long after this interview that we've just watched that you were able to leave Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12 hours later -- no, 24. The next morning, officials of the Autonomous Region of Krajina arrived. And after an interview that was conducted, I was ordered to leave for Banja Luka with Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's take this in stages. You say: "officials from the Autonomous Region of Krajina arrived." How many officials, first of all? One or more than one?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw two cars and some police escort. They parked outside the restaurant that we were able to see on the photographs. So there were several people, and some police escort, as I said, in two vehicles. I was not able to see them from the distance. It was only later when the guards came to fetch me to take me to the administration building, I saw only one person directly, Mr. Kupresanin. When we set out for Banja Luka, only Mr. Kupresanin's vehicle went. The other one remained. I don't know who was in this other vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were taken to the administration building, and you saw Mr. Kupresanin. Had you met him before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had. That is, he was a member of the BH parliament, as myself. So we sometimes talked or had a cup of coffee during the breaks in parliamentary sessions. But let me add, when he entered the room in which I was waiting, I thought he was someone else. He asked me whether I remembered him, and I said: "Yes, from the Municipal Assembly" because it was -- I couldn't believe that someone else could be there apart from officials from Prijedor. But he introduced himself. He said who he was, Vojo Kupresanin, the president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and he said: "I remember you very well from the BH assembly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he explain to you why he was there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything specific about the reasons for his being there. When he got in, and when he started talking to me, he proceeded with some political arguments and political theories. I just listened to him. I didn't say anything. But at one point, he was called out. A soldier came, and he said that the president wanted to talk to him over the telephone. So he left the room, and I was able to hear parts of the conversation. He said on two occasions that they needed 300 beds, a lot of soap and detergent, and I realised that he had come to see what the situation was because obviously, they were preparing something, because he had requested for this number of beds to be brought to the camp. But I didn't ask anything. It was only later on the way to Banja Luka that I was able to glean some further information from our conversation in the car. But it was only at the end when he took me to their government building in Banja Luka that I realised what it was all about. He had talked to Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pause there. Right. This is what I want to come back to. You told us that a soldier came whilst he was in the room with you in Omarska and said that the president wanted to talk to him. Did he use the word "president" or did he use the name of the man?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure at this point. I don't know whether he said "President Karadzic" or "president" only. I really cannot tell you this. I know that he said one interesting thing. He said I found only one. This is what I clearly remember having heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said "I found only one"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupresanin said, while talking on the telephone to the president with whom he was speaking. He mentioned beds, soap, bedsheets and so on and so forth. And he said: "I've found only one." I thought that he meant me, but I wasn't sure at that moment. Later, I was convinced that he was referring to myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, so he talked to the president on the telephone. Then he came back to the room. At what stage did you realise you were going to be taken out of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this telephone conversation was over, he came back to the room in which I sat, and he said: "You have to come with me." I didn't know where. He didn't say where. And since at that moment I thought that that was my end, the end of my life, I wanted at least to go to the glass house and tell the people there that I was being taken away. I found some pretext for that, and I asked Mr. Kupresanin: "Can I go and fetch my clothes?" He said: "You will no longer need it." And then added: "At any rate, they are dirty, and you don't need them." I asked him once again, and then he said: "Well, go and get it." As we were going down the stairs of the administration building, he said: "You better hurry up, because we're leaving for Banja Luka now." I went to the glass house. Quickly I took my jacket, and I told the people there that they were taking me to Banja Luka. I was convinced at that time that they would take me to the Tunjica prison in the area of Banja Luka, but as soon as I got into the car, he explained to me that -- not mentioning the prison -- that I would be able to get some rest now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he explain where he was going to take you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said the following: "Now, we have to find Mirza Mujadzic, Rasema Cero, and he asked me whether I knew where they were. I said that Mrs. Cero was in Sarajevo and that Mujadzic was in Bihac. He said: "Well, in that case, we have to find your family. Until that time, you will be in a Serb village in perfect safety, where you will be able to get some rest, gain some weight. And then, after that, we will try to organise some round tables which I will then attend on behalf of the Muslim people." That's the way he put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause a minute there. He asked you where Mirza Mujadzic was, and also where Rasim Cero. Who was the second? Who was that lady?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This lady was an MP in the BH parliament. She comes from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He told you that you were going to be placed into a Serb village. Did you actually go to Banja Luka itself, however, first?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He took me to the building -- either the municipality building, the assembly building, or the government building. I don't know exactly which. But it was the seat of the authorities of the autonomous region, and perhaps some other institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you were there, in whatever this building was, did you hear another conversation between Mr. Kupresanin and someone else?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was the conversation between President Karadzic and Mr. Kupresanin. He repeated similar things that he had already said in Omarska over the telephone. He said he had brought me, that I was the only one he had been able to find. He said that he would get me a suit, find me a job, give me some money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, how did you know that the person at the other end of the phone was Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Kupresanin who said that he was talking to Karadzic, and one could hear his voice, a high-pitched voice that one could hear over this very old telephone. And he said: "Well, I'm talking to the president now." And the president said that I should be enabled to have some rest and put on some weight. But he didn't tell me the reason they were doing this in specific. He did not say anything in detail. He only mentioned this round table, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand from the conversation you overheard, for example, that he had only found one, and that you would participate in a round table? What did you understand was the purpose of you being taken out of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obvious to me that after the arrival, after the visit of the foreign journalists, Kupresanin went to Omarska. I don't know what he discussed with the camp authorities. But he found only me, although it was obvious that he had been looking for other people as well. He asked about Mujadzic and Rasema Cero, that is, the MPs in the BH assembly from this area. It seemed logical to me that they had some kind of political plan to use the politicians who had survived, the people who had had some kind of political function before. It was from the driver of the car who had been ordered to take me to Vrbanja, to the house of my sister, who -- that I got some additional information. This driver, totally unprompted, turned around and told me: "I think it's very wise of you to have decided to become an MP in the Serbian assembly. But it is also very dangerous for you because Muslim extremists might kill you." So he confirmed my suspicions. I concluded that Kupresanin had probably received orders to find political officials, politicians, and to use them and to present them as members of the Serbian assembly, members who were of non-Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And were you, in fact, then, taken to Vrbanja and found accommodation there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They put me in the house of my brother-in-law and my sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just before we leave that, was Vrbanja -- was kind of a place was Vrbanja? Was it ethnically mixed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost entire Vrbanja is actually an area which used to be inhabited by Muslim and, to a smaller extent, Croat population. It was only the surrounding areas, the approaches to the town, that were inhabited by Serb population. It is located on the outskirts of Banja Luka, on the eastern side of Banja Luka. It was actually a suburb of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the light of the evidence that you've given to this Court about Trnopolje and Omarska, I'd like you to have a look, please, at a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it bears the 65 ter number 322. Your Honour, it was a late addition to the bundle, so it will probably be at the back. I'm told by Ms. Karper that it would have been in a separate bundle from the main bundle that was handed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it please could be presented on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly. We can hand the witness the copy in B/C/S, and we've got an English copy to go on the ELMO, if the usher takes it from us to save time. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence has a copy? We are all in the same problem. Please understand we received here four or five bundles, and we can't bring it along always. So is the Defence prepared to proceed without the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We would prefer to have it, obviously, Your Honour, but whatever way the Court and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is Your Honour intending -- I'm not sure what time Your Honour takes the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We may have the break now, and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll arrange for further copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. And then the trial stands adjourned until 5.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. I know that it is a point of concern of the OTP that a special file will never be lost, and therefore let's turn immediately to this file. I'm sure that the Defence had the possibility to look into this document called "originals for Court" and it's on some documents bearing a signature, to put it very neutral. The Bench would ask the OTP to provide for colour copies of these documents on the -- of the front and back side, that we can come back to these documents later on. The Judges have decided not to go into details of this document before July 1st, for obvious reasons. Therefore, it doesn't mean that the Judges do not insist on having expert witness, graphologist, especially on the following documents: 64, 66, 68, 69, 71, 72, 75, 77, 78, 46, 81, 82, 85. We expect if any observations -- additional observations by the parties as said in the beginning of July, if there is no clarification in addition until then, it seems indispensable for the Judges to have an expert witness on these signatures we have available. But please provide colour copies for all parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just mention, Your Honour, I don't think we need to go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the usher please give this back to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- In the event that Your Honours, that it does come to a stage that expert evidence is required, we will be requesting Your Honours or we will be asking the Defence first for samples of handwriting. We can't conduct a comparison without samples. But Your Honour, I'm mentioning that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think let's discuss this later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, very quickly before we go back to what's a lengthy document in fact, raise one matter, and it's just for clarification. In respect of the witness, the videolink, we have a joint recollection. Your Honours had fixed a date which was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no, no. Not to be misunderstood, it was not fixing a date. It was just saying it would be excellent if it would be possible at that date, but it's not any kind of an order. Of course, we should wait until July 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, but the only reason I'm asking is because it takes I'm told something in the region of three weeks to set this up, so we need to aim for a date. And that is, in fact -- Your Honour I'm not going to pre-empt matters, we're going to have to discuss how this witness can be fitted into the Brdjanin/Talic case as well. But we will aim for that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Observations on this from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not on this point, but on others the Court has made, we will reserve those for a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is necessary for today immediately, with regard to the witness before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please, let's proceed with the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think Your Honours have now all got copies of the document. But perhaps we had better just have the English version on the ELMO. Your Honours, because it's a very lengthy document, I am again going to select parts to read out. But Your Honour, it is a document that we would want to get it in full at some stage as opposed to Your Honour maybe admitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But in this case, please take into account that we have two official languages in this Tribunal, and provide a French translation as well, probably it will be necessary for another case as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will. We will submit this for as quick a French translation as we can get. And in addition to that, Your Honour, I have spoken to counsel for General Talic, who are going to see -- they did get some documents translated, and they are going to check which ones they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's really mutual cooperation in criminal matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I want you to look at this document, because then I want to ask you some questions about it based on your experiences. It is from the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, or rather -- I beg your pardon. It's at the request of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre. The Prijedor public security station made a report on reception centres in the Prijedor Municipality. The request from the chief or the decision was dated the 14th of August, 1992. The report begins with some background information. It states that "we consider it necessary to point out that on the 29th, 30th of April, 1992, the SDS and its forces assumed power in all organs and throughout the municipality. In this manner, Prijedor Municipality has formally joined the Krajina region, that is to say, the Serbian Republic." And it then set out the areas within the Prijedor Municipality which were inhabited by Muslims and those populated by Muslims and Croats. It then goes on to set out the decisions -- this is in paragraph 2 -- that "the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic adopted a decision to disarm all paramilitary units, groups, and individuals" whilst urging citizens to conduct those actions in a peaceful and civilised way without any consequences for those possessing weapons. Again, I'm going to omit this for the time being. It talked about the negotiations that went on. And then in the middle of the second paragraph, gives their version or its version of the attack, the incident in Hambarine. "At the beginning of May," the sentence begins, "the extremists provoked the first incident in the village of Hambarine when they stopped a group of soldiers without any reason. On that occasion they resorted to using their weapons, killing three and seriously injuring two soldiers. After the brutal attack, the extremists fled their houses with their weapons. The residents of Hambarine rejected any sort of cooperation with the civilian and military authorities in connection with their arrest and taken into custody." And then it goes on to say: "Since the residents of the village of Hambarine did not abide by the decision of the Ministry of the People's Defence of the Serbian Republic and did not surrender their weapons, refused to cooperate with legal authorities regarding the attack against the soldiers, and rejected the demands set by the army, the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality decided to intervene militarily in the village, in order to disarm and apprehend those known to have perpetrated the crime against the soldiers. The army intervened, but did not find the attackers. Instead, it only established the Prijedor/Ljubija Road communication and placed the village of Hambarine under its control. The Muslim extremists resisted, but this time the army suffered no losses." "However, on the 24th of May, 1992, Muslim extremists in the village of Jakupovici used their weapons to attack a military patrol, wounding a soldier. Troops from Prijedor set out to assist the patrol, but the armed Muslim extremists attempted to stop them at the first Muslim houses at the edge of Prijedor. On that occasion, a fierce armed clash broke out between the army and the Muslim extremists in the broader Kozarac area. The Muslims refused to surrender their weapons, and subsequently it was established that they had extensively prepared for the armed conflict over a long period of time." "During the fighting, the army left a free corridor for all citizens who wanted to take shelter and flee from the zone of armed conflict, that is to say, for all those who did not want to take part in an armed struggle against the army of the Serbian Republic. The army organised shelter for such citizens in the village of Trnopolje, in the elementary school, the social centre, warehouse, and neighbouring houses, to ensure their safety. This is how the open reception centre of Trnopolje was established, and it continues to operate to this day. The name itself equates the nature of the centre in which, as the conflict broke out, citizens of all ages, both male and female, took shelter. The centre has no barbed wire fence. No investigations are conducted in it. The army secures the centre from attacks by extremists." Now can we stop there for a moment, Mr. Sejmenovic. First of all, "the centre has no barbed wire fence." True or not true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre was partly surrounded by barbed wire. A part of the fence was made of metal, and there was a part where there was no fence, no metal fence and no barbed wire fence. I have already given a detailed account of this in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. The fence that we saw in the film against which the people were standing, was that the part that you say was partly surrounded by barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the part which did have the barbed wire before. Whether it had been there in the same length before the war, I can't say. But I know that a part of the agricultural community warehouse was surrounded by barbed wire. It's possible that it was connected with this other fence later on during these events. But I can't say this for sure because I never stayed very close to that fence, not during the period I'm now talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. "No investigations are conducted in it." True or not true, as far as you know, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, it's not true because I was questioned myself. There was a small room there within the local commune building where men were regularly questioned, many of them were beaten, and some of them succumbed to the consequences of these beatings there. This information I obtained from people who were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you obtained from people who were in the camp whilst you yourself were there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then: "The army secures the centre from attacks by extremists." What was your understanding of the role of the army there? You've told us about the machine-gun nests.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army set up guards around the camp and the machine-gun nests. The camp was also run, governed, by the military. Occasionally, as I've already said, I did see a couple of policemen coming to the camp in their blue uniforms, but only very seldom. Concerning those who were there on a permanent basis, who were taking people away, questioning people, and who were securing the camp, all of them were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What this report appears to say is the army was protecting the inmates of Trnopolje from attacks by what's described as "extremists". Was that the impression that you got, that the army was there to protect the inmates?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour I'll object to the form of the question. If counsel is testifying what it appears to her, perhaps she can do it at a later time in the proceedings, but this witness has already testified to what he believes it is and answered a question which is both compound and improper in its form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained. Already previously I indicated that such kind of questions can't be really answered by the witness because the witness can't know what is in the heads of persons who laid down these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but can I -- I mean, I'll simply ask this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask the question, did you get the impression, forgetting about what the report says, did you get the impression that the army was there to protect the inmates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. This is fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I respect the Court's ruling on it, but just for the record, if I may comment, it's a little too late once the horse has left the barn, to ask this witness to review a document which he has never testified before, and then to come back to it and say, well, let's try it in a different fashion now, by saying let's forget about this document and what it says in front of you, what do you think the impression is? I know what the answer is, I think everyone who's going to hear the testimony -- he will say exactly what the document says. It's a complete farce to ask a question like that. Counsel had an opportunity to inquire of his thoughts throughout the entire Trnopolje camp, and now we've passed that. We're in a new document now, having read the document, how can we or how can this panel of judges now distinguish between what he thought at the time, what he thought after reviewing the document, or now what he thought ten years later having reviewed the document, whether or not the army secured it for purposes of the extremists or for whatever reason it may be. I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to waste time. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no. Let me just state. To avoid this discussion in the future, once again, both parties please be aware, you don't have a jury in front of you; you have three Judges. And I wonder if you wouldn't be interested to hear what is our summary of what we obtain as evidence, and I think you can rely that we know to distinguish in detail. And therefore, as it was done in the past, everybody should have a second chance, and it was granted. Also in the past, to the Defence. Please, may the Prosecutor continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'll move on, Your Honour. I don't want to waste more time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just look at the next sentence: "The number of citizens staying there varies because those who wish to can leave the centre at any time since there is a railway station located right by it." Mr. Sejmenovic, whilst you were there, were people leaving the -- leaving Trnopolje, using the railway station?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by their own desire, because that's what is stated here, and that's not true. There was a very precise procedure for the setting up of convoys. It was known whom the Serb authorities had allowed to leave at the beginning it was only women and children. But sometimes, freight cars would be sent to the railway station, and sometimes later on empty buses and lorries arrived. At any rate, men could not cross the fence of the camp of their own free will, or to suit their own needs. That was only at a later date, based on approvals that they would then obtain from the camp command or from the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, moving on, he says -- the report says in August, there are about 1500 Muslim citizens. "They have organised themselves with respect to accommodation and food, and they are assisted by the army and the Red Cross." Again, whilst you were there and from what you understood, what was the organisation, with respect to accommodation and food?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no organisation of accommodation and food. People were allowed to sleep inside the school building, the gym, the old cinema hall, and on the meadow surrounding the complex. That was allowed. Later on, people were allowed to organise their food themselves. Fires were lit and used to cook food, and we had common cauldrons. But this food was not provided by the Serbian authorities, but by individual inmates who had been granted approval to leave the camp in order to forage for runaway cattle or to find flour in the houses surrounding the camp and bring it back to the camp, to organise the provisions of food. So nothing organised at the camp level except for provisional authorisations to go to the surrounding houses and search for food there. As far as medical care is concerned, while I was at the camp, I never went to the medical unit because it was dangerous for me to go to that side of the camp. But I did hear that the doctor we saw on the -- we saw in the footage, and another veterinary, a lady veterinary, and another doctor called Jusuf Pasic were trying to provide basic medical assistance to people. In what measure, in what way exactly, I had no opportunity to see. But I know that this sort of thing did exist. Later on, the Serbian Red Cross started coming to the camp from Prijedor. I did not know at that time that the Red Cross provided food for the camp. While I was there, people were still receiving permits to go to their own houses, not half a kilometre from the camp, to fetch some flour and bring it back to the camp. I saw some of that with my own eyes, people who were allowed to go to their gardens, which were a couple of hundred yards from the camp, get the vegetables from the garden, and then prepare the vegetables inside the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just kindly interrupt. The witness has given already a very detailed and long description of his own experiences, and the Judges do not believe that it's added value to have once again an echo on the basis of that what can be read in this document. And therefore, it seems not to be necessary. It is from our perspective for the Judges to compare that what we can read here opposed to what we heard already by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take the point. I was going to ask the witness to move. I just want to ask one question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw in that video what appeared to be a Red Cross person, a nurse, being interviewed. Was that a member of the Serbian Red Cross, are you able to say, or of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe she belonged to the Serbian Red Cross from Prijedor, and that she was a Serb by nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let's just move on. And there are a couple of other questions I want to ask you on that, but we'll just look at what else it says. It goes on to talk about, as you've already mentioned, the clinic with a medical team on duty round the clock, equipped to extend basic medical care, and that patients with more serious ailments are transported to the medical centre in Prijedor or Banja Luka. And then states that "The open reception centre will probably have to remain open for some time to come." It then moves on to deal, this report, with the conflict as it's called in Kozarac. "Since armed conflict broke out in the broader Kozarac area between armed Muslim extremists who, according to information received subsequently, numbered around 4.000 men..." Pausing there, you've already told us there was some arming of the TO. Was there in your estimation anything -- well, 4.000 men is the figure given. What do you say was closest?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 4.000 people, the figure makes no sense because we are talking about 4.000 armed persons here. Militarily speaking, there may have been a couple of hundreds of people who were armed. If we take into account improvised weapons, handmade pistols, hunting rifles. Even so, I think it was at the very most a quarter of the number mentioned here. I can't really tell because I didn't count those weapons. But I can speak about the area in which I was staying, so there were very few armed persons there. The inspector at the Omarska camp told me himself that we had very few weapons and that that really wasn't what he was interested in. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then let's look at what else is said. "Numbered around 4.000 men, and the army of the Serbian Republic, a large number of persons were captured in combat; that is to say, on the territory in which combat operations took place. Despite the fact that the Muslim extremists extended fierce armed resistance and ruthlessly settled accounts with those members of their own ethnic group who refused to fight the Serbian forces." Now, do you know anything about apparently Muslims ruthlessly settling accounts with other Muslims who refused to fight?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary, Your Honours. As I have explained before, we offered every person of military age to join the Territorial Defence of their own free will, or not to do so. People did it on a voluntary basis, and signed their names on a voluntary basis. Those who didn't sign were not considered part of the TO, nor am I familiar with anyone exercising any sort of pressure for other people to join the TO or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. The Judges have decided that on page 68, line 20, beginning with the word "I" until line 23 has to be struck out from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's the position it's an opinion not in the sphere of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. I'm sorry. I was looking at something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour. I'd like to heard on this matter, but it would take some time, so I'd like, before the Court directs -- and I know you already have -- perhaps we can revisit this at the start of the proceedings tomorrow at 2.15 because we do have a position on it and it will take some time to explain to the Court. And I think it would be better left outside the presence of the witness, with your permission obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Recalling your previous submissions, we regard it necessary to intervene at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And therefore, it may be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just interested to know, Your Honour, whether Your Honour can do the same in Your Honours' own jurisdiction. I know the Americans can, but we can't. I'm quite interested by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, right. I'm sorry, Mr. Sejmenovic. Yes, you dealt with that. Oh yes, sorry, yes, "refused to fight the Serbian forces. The local authorities, the army and even the police were not prepared for such developments, believing to the very end in a peaceful and civilised agreement between ethnic communities, so that the problem of providing shelter and safety for employed persons emerged. In such a situation, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality decided to utilize the facilities of the Keraterm work organisation in Prijedor to accommodate those captured under the supervision of the employees of the Prijedor public security station and the Prijedor military police. The Prijedor public security station, aware of its personnel possibilities and the seriousness of the newly emerged problem, informed the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, and the command of the Banja Luka Corps and asked for help and specialised personnel to operatively process those captured. The Banja Luka services centre and the command of the Banja Luka Corps became actively in resolving the situation. They sent a large number of experienced professionals to Prijedor whereupon mixed teams consisting of a members of national, public and military security were established, with the task of carrying out the operative processing of captured persons and determining, for each individual, the degree of personal responsibility in the armed rebellion. Operative processing was initiated in the Keraterm facility in Prijedor to which the army brought around 600 persons at the beginning of the conflict. "However, armed conflicts spread to other areas of the municipality, and the number of captured persons increased unexpectedly. It was obvious that given the limited capacities of this facility, as well as for security reasons, it was not opportune to continue keeping detainees in this facility. For this reason, the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality decided that all detainees from Keraterm in Prijedor be transferred to the premises of the administration building and workshop of the iron ore mine in Omarska where mixed teams of operative personnel would continue the initiated processing, which is why this facility was given the working title "Omarska Investigative Centre for Prisoners of War." On the basis of the same decision, the facility was placed under the supervision of the police and army." Mr. Sejmenovic, pausing there for a moment, in your stay in Omarska, whilst you were in the glass house and elsewhere, did you meet people who had been captured in combat, fighting, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "On the basis of the same decision, the facility was placed under the supervision of the police and army. The police were thus entrusted with the task of providing direct physical security, while the army provided in-depth security in the form of two circles, and by laying mines along the potential routes of escape by prisoners. Certain facilities in Omarska were supplied with water and had the necessary number of toilet facilities and washrooms, a mess hall, and large rooms in which the detainees were to sleep, as well as a sufficient number of offices in which processing was performed." Mr. Sejmenovic, pausing again, was the glass house supplied with water?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the glass house wasn't. The so-called "water centre" at the juncture between the restaurant, the glass house, and the administration was. There were improvised water taps on the ground floor which had previously been used for the workers to wash their hands and to drink water. It was situated adjacent to the restaurant, and that's how it had been before the war. As far as the neighbouring facilities are concerned, there was no such thing there, that they only had hangars there for repairing dumpers, big lorries. There were several cisterns there with industrial water which was not drinking water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It then goes on to talk about the mess hall and large rooms in which the detainee where is to sleep. "With the exception of posting guards and organising sleeping facilities to the detainees, no other modifications were performed at the facility, so there was no barbed wire around it, while the existing rooms were used for work with the detainees. Basic medical care was organised, food was prepared in the kitchen at the Omarska iron ore mine and distributed in the restaurant via a self-service system to the detainees, personnel, and some of the iron ore mine workers who stayed on to maintain the facility. "The same decision of the Crisis Staff decrees the Keraterm facility in Prijedor shall be used exclusively as a transit camp and only the first selection of those taken into custody shall be carried out there, since this cannot be done in the Prijedor public security station as a result of limited facilities." Now, on the basis of the decision referred to above, on the 27th of May, 1992, all prisoners of war were transferred to Omarska, and then new ones were brought in, whether they were captured in combat or taken into custody on the basis of the results of operative processing. After criminal investigation processing --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you pause a minute for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Normally, it comes up on the screen when I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "After criminal investigation processing, the operatives separated all persons brought to Omarska into three categories, depending on the degree of personal responsibility in the armed rebellion. The first category included persons suspected of the most serious crimes and those who directly organised and took part in the armed rebellion. The second category included persons suspected of organising, assisting, and financing armed rebellion. The third category included persons who were not interesting from a security point of view, but who were captured because they found themselves in combat zones, although in the course of investigation, it was established that they were forced to stay in the area by extremists. Likewise, this category included those for whom there was no substantial proof that they had participated in the armed rebellion in any manner whatsoever." Mr. Sejmenovic, the people that you met, which category did they fall into?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the people in the glass house? Or anywhere in the camp?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Let's deal with the people in the glass house first.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who belonged to which category, nor did I learn from my partial contacts with those people whether they knew which group they belonged to. Only the camp authorities really knew that, the inspectors who questioned those people and who determined where to put a certain person in as far as they had any such categories at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's my fault. The question was not clear enough. Did the people that you met, did anybody admit or tell you that they had organised or had anything to do with an armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet anyone who admitted to organising or assisting or financing any arming of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see some individuals who were members of the Territorial Defence for whom I know that fact and whom I knew by sight. I saw several such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third category, as the Serbs categorized them, were those who were captured because they found themselves in what is called "combat zones." How many people that you met fell into that category?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say once again that we could not identify the categories. We didn't know who belonged to which category, but I did recognise a number of people there from various parts of the municipality, including young people and elderly people. I'm referring to the area of Kozarac and Hambarine. There were no people left there. They were all either in Omarska or Trnopolje or Keraterm camp. So the overall male population was in one of these three locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody forced, in the Kozarac area, while you were there, to remain in the area although they wanted to leave, by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There was no one there who could have forced them to leave, even if they had wanted to. It was the Serb military who entered the area, arrested people, or told the population that they had to go to Trnopolje, else they would be killed. Others were taken to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Pause there a second. It's my fault again. What I'm asking you is not whether people wanted to leave, but were people forced to remain, for example, in the area of Kozarac by members of the Muslim TO? In other words, ordinary citizens, at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Absolutely not. The people were forced by the Serb military to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just finishing the document off, then: "According to the available documents and files kept in Omarska, from the 27th of May, to the 16th of August, a total of 3.334 persons were brought to the investigative centre of which 3.197 were Muslim, 125 were Croat, 11 were Serbs, 1 was an other, there were 28 people under the age of 18, 68 over 60, 2.920 between 18 and 60, 3.297 males, and 37 women. During their stay in the investigations centre, two persons, both Muslim, died of natural causes. In the period from the 27th of May to the 16th of August, 1992, a total of 49 persons left the centre in an unknown manner and in an unknown direction. "From 27 May to the 16th of August, 3.334 persons underwent criminal investigation processing in the centre. Of this number, 1.773 were transferred to Trnopolje, and 1.331 to the military camp at Manjaca, along with the collected documentation on the degree of responsibility in participating in the armed rebellion. And currently 179 persons are being processed in the Omarska reception centre." And then it deals with the continuing investigation. And finally, on citizens moving out from the Prijedor Municipality: "According to intelligence obtained by the Prijedor Public Security Station, and on the basis of public rumours, there are grounds to believe that 4.000 to 5.000 persons, primarily Muslims, had moved away from the Prijedor Municipality before armed conflict broke out." Yes. "This public security station has no official data concerning the matter since these persons gave no official notice of departure from their residences in keeping with the regulations. Furthermore, according to information which has not been adequately verified, it is suspected that this group primarily included members of the immediate families of the most extreme advocates of armed conflicts with the Serbs, and that by removing their families, that is to say, having them to move to other areas, they were able to devote themselves to the fullest extent to preparations for war." Pausing there, Mr. Sejmenovic, were you aware of people in your area sending their families away so that they could devote themselves to preparation for war? That is, non-Serb families.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it says: "From the onset of the armed conflict in the municipality to this day, according to insufficiently verified data, around 20.000 citizens of all ages, both male and female, primarily Muslim and Croat, but also Serb, have moved away from the municipality." And then it deals with -- well, perhaps I better read the rest. "The public security station does not have at its disposal official documents on this group either, since they left the municipality without giving official notice of departure from their place of residence. They mostly used trains as transport to Doboj, private vehicles to drive off in all directions, or other means of transport. "At present, on the 16th of August, 1992, at the request of residents, the Prijedor Public Security Station has issued notice of termination of residence to 13.180 residents who issued requests in keeping with the legal regulations. This group has still not moved away from the municipality but has only given notice of departure from their residences. With the assistance of religious and humanitarian organisations, they are currently seeking ways to move away, exclusively to Slovenia or other western countries. The Prijedor Public Security Station does not have at its disposal data indicating what these persons have done with their real estate or what they have done or intend to do with their moveable property. In this respect, the public security station employees will carry out every request issued by the authorised organs of the Serbian Republic in conformity with the rights and obligations deriving from the scope of the work of internal affairs organs. 280 Serbian families were the area of the Cazin Krajina have settled in Prijedor Municipality in the area of the village of Trnopolje. Discussions are currently underway that 400 Serbian families from the broader Zenica area also be settled in the same village." I want to come back a little later to what happened in Trnopolje. And then finally, the activities of the Prijedor station. "The Serbian employees of the public security station, both active and in reserve, have jointly participated in a systematic manner in assuming authority which was successfully executed on the 29th/30th of April, and subsequently most of the time was devoted to ensuring the physical security of vital facilities in the municipality." And then they deal with the police -- "after the outbreak of armed conflict, at the army's request and as a result of the situation which they confronted, public security station employees directly participated in armed conflicts. So far, 11 persons on active-duty or reservists have lost their lives, while a total of 38 have been wounded. "Together with members of military units, police employees are participating in combing and mopping up terrain with respect to enemy groups and individuals who have remained behind or have concealed themselves. Through intelligence field work, they are obtaining useful information on the enemy's activity in the municipality." And I think I don't need to read anything else. And it is signed by Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But quite frankly, I find, based on what the witness testified, which was redacted why the OTP would want a self-serving, distorted, inaccurate document, as this witness has called it to be introduced in as evidence. I think that it's irrelevant, and I do not think it should be accepted, based on this witness's testimony, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: At any rate, it's necessary to have this document, for a better understanding of the transcript, and in the understanding that the Office of the Prosecutor will provide the original and colour copy of page 9 of the B/C/S version. This document is admitted into evidence as S152A in the English version, and B in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If Your Honour could give me one minute, I just want to check... Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you now be shown the document with the 65 ter number 365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In which bundle can we find this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The big bundle, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I can deal with other matters. Your Honour, I'm told it's already been gone through. It's S90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it's from list 2 and the other. S90. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, just looking at this document which was the minutes of the session of the national Defence council of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly held at 1200 on the 29th of September and presided over by Dr. Milomir Stakic, it has already been read, so I just want to look at Item 2 on the agenda. "The National Defence Council will take on all the essential obligations regarding the unhindered arrival of all persons from the Open Trnopolje Reception Centre according to a list agreed by the municipal Red Cross and International Red Cross. The public security station would provide escort, vehicles, and fuel via the secretariat for fuel and economy -- via the secretariat for economy and social services, and three, the municipal Red Cross will be advised to close down the Open Trnopolje Reception Centre as the departure of all registered persons from this reception centre effectively makes it unnecessary." By this stage, Mr. Sejmenovic, you were out of Omarska. Did you hear about the closure of the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, just to interrupt once again. It's not correct what you stated that it's already gone through and read out. We haven't come to this point yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I thought it had been read out. Does Your Honour want me to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, and if it's necessary from your point of view, you may add additional parts or portions from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just go back, then, to establish that it shows that the session was, as I said, was presided over by Dr. Stakic and was attended by him, Mr. Savanovic, Dr. Kovacevic, Radmilo Zeljaja, Bosko Mandic, Slavko Budimir, Ranko Travar, Simo Drljaca, and Milenko Rajlic. And the agenda included a report on the forthcoming activities regarding the open Trnopolje reception centre, and then the bits that I have just read out were dealt with, were the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I'm sorry. Did you become aware of the closure of Trnopolje? Rather, I should say again, I'll rephrase that question. That a large number of people were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the period indicated above, that is, when these minutes were taken on the 29th of September, 1992, I did not have this information. While we were there in Trnopolje, from time to time, we were told that the whole camp would be evacuated in this way. When I departed from this area and arrived in Banja Luka, I no longer had any information on what was going on in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In that case, I'll leave that. I want now to deal -- I may ask you about some more documents tomorrow, but I want now to deal with what happened to you after you had been released from Omarska. You said that you went to Vrbanja and stayed in a house, I think you said, with -- was it your sister? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had been there a couple of days, did you see Mr. Kupresanin again?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was taken to Vrbanja by Mr. Kupresanin, an officer, and the driver. I was in this car. They wanted to talk to my sister and my brother-in-law first, and then to leave me in their house. They arrived in Vrbanja. They had this talk with them. I stayed behind, and they went back to Banja Luka. After that, they visited Vrbanja on several occasions. Before that, they had taken me to Banja Luka on three occasions, if remember it correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. I want to come to when you saw Mr. Kupresanin again.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I mean, several days after my arrival in Vrbanja, soldiers came and took me to Mr. Kupresanin once again, to the government building in Banja Luka. Again, I had a conversation with Kupresanin and a similar thing occurred on several more occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you about one particular occasion when -- I'm sorry. Before I do that, what was the purpose of taking you to see Mr. Kupresanin on this -- the number of occasions at the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first occasion, Kupresanin wanted me to establish a telephone contact with the BH Army, that is, with the authorities in Sarajevo. And then in particular, with the authorities in Tuzla. He tried to talk me into that. I must say that he did not exert any physical pressure on me, but he wanted me to talk to the authorities there because he said whenever they made such an attempt, they would cut off. And he said that he needed me to establish this contact in Tuzla as well. On the second occasion, when I was taken there, he said that it was only to give me some food by way of assistance. And on the third occasion, I was taken there for the purpose of meeting Dr. Radovan Karadzic who visited Banja Luka on that day, and also for the purposes of meeting Cyrus Vance and Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, you were taken there. Was that said to you in advance, for the purpose of meeting Karadzic, Vance, and Carrington?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupresanin and a couple of other officers came to Bosanska Vrbanja, Kupresanin told me that I had very little time to get ready. That I had to shave and change the clothes that I was wearing at the moment. He added: "You're now going to see President Karadzic. You will have a talk with him. And afterwards, you will probably meet with some other people." I don't remember him saying that I would meet with Cyrus Vance and Lord Carrington. But I heard it over the radio that this high-ranking international delegation had already arrived in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Municipal Assembly building, were there members -- first of all, were there a number of people at the building?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many people there. We spent some time in the corridor on the second or the first floor. I'm not sure. We stood there for a while. And more and more people were coming in. Some 20 minutes later, or less, a very great number of people had gathered, civilians, officers. I recognised a number of politicians amongst them, the people I knew from the parliament. I saw a number of MPs. I stood there next to Kupresanin and waited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were a number of politicians, people you knew from parliament. Did you see any politicians from the Prijedor area in particular?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I first saw Mr. Srdjo Srdic, an MP in the Bosnian parliament while it was still functioning. After that, I saw Dr. Stakic, who came some 10 minutes after Mr. Srdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came up the stairs to the corridor where we were, and he came up to me and greeted me. He saw Mr. Srdic. I believe he greeted him, too, without exchanging too many words. And afterwards, he went in the direction of the offices. He stood there, down there, for a while, and then he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say he saw Mr. Srdic. Was there any conversation at that stage that you heard between Stakic and Srdic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no conversation between Stakic and Srdic. They just briefly greeted each other, and then Mr. Stakic went away. Mr. Srdic stayed behind. From time to time, he would approach a group of people, and then come back. At one point, he left. I must say that there was a big argument going on amongst these people who had gathered in the corridor. They were criticising Mr. Karadzic, and Srdic criticised him most, for having delegated power, for having -- he said that not all of the agreements had been implemented. He spoke about some buses. And he denied his responsibility in respect of these buses. At one moment, he came up to me. He took me by my hand, and he took me to this other group of people. And he said: "Mevludin, please tell them, please confirm that I never set foot in Omarska or Keraterm. I don't want to be held responsible for anything. I had nothing to do with those buses."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let's pause there for a moment. Do you know what buses he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time. I think that he mentioned Vlasic on that occasion, but I simply didn't know. But since they were talking about Prijedor and since I had been able to see evacuations, such evacuations from time to time, I sensed that there was something wrong with this deportation. When I came back several days later, the international media had already published the fact that massacres had occurred in the area of Mount Vlasic. So I made a connection between these two things, and I realised why Srdic had reacted the way he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was Srdic -- you say that he was criticising, or they were, Mr. Karadzic, and Srdic criticised him most for having delegated power. Was he saying anything about the municipalities and Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srdic was cursing Karadzic. He was saying something to the effect that Karadzic had given all the power to the presidents of the municipalities and that they were acting on their own. This is what he was saying. He said that he had disbanded the regions, the autonomous regions. And as a result of that, the sole authority lied in the hands of the municipal presidents. He further spoke about the burning of the houses in Cela and Gomjenica, something that had not been agreed upon earlier on. He mentioned cases of arson in Ljubija. I believe that he spoke about some Croatian houses that had been burned down in Zune, I think, and he complained about Stakic and Stakic's men, as he said. Privately, he also complained about the fact that Stakic's men had or had intended to burn down his house, which was located in the vicinity of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we can't conclude without announcing a decision of the Bench. We have before us a witness now concluding the fourth day of the testimony. In advance, the Judges were told that the estimated time would be four hours. We have really to concentrate on the main issues of the case; and therefore, time limit is necessary. The Chamber regards it as adequate to finalise the testimony of this witness no later than 90 minutes after the start of tomorrow's hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ostojic asked Your Honour for time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We start tomorrow immediately without any further discussions, and then we have 90 minutes to go with this witness. It's also, from the point of the witness, impossible to continue to continue. And a possible way is not to introduce too many documents through a witness, but to come to the concrete facts and to that what the witness has experienced. And this is what the Judges really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sent a message to Your Honour asking if I could discuss this, as Mr. Ostojic did earlier, before this witness came in the reason why I'm doing this. And there really is a good reason. Your Honour, I don't know if we can have five minutes out of the interpreters, and perhaps the witness can leave because I really want to explain the reason why I'm doing this. I'd like the opportunity to do that before Your Honour makes a final ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have made our ruling, and we proceed this way tomorrow without any further discussion. We have to conclude this witness. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
